title: A welcome thaw in an icy Arctic issue
text:
A welcome thaw in an icy Arctic issue
A new agreement over Greenland’s status, and U.S. access to the island, shows that quiet diplomacy can help Western allies move from icy relations to more stability in countering common foes.
The United States, Denmark, and the semiautonomous Danish territory of Greenland are poised to sign a new deal on the Arctic island’s future. In an announcement on Friday, President Donald Trump lauded the step as “a dream come true for the United States of America.”
The response from other leaders has been low-key, but positive, with an apparent consensus that it’s time to move on from the instability caused by U.S. threats of a forcible takeover of Greenland. In addition, this development shows that behind-the-scenes diplomacy can still be effective, even in an atmosphere of decreasing trust among allies.
“A win for quiet professionalism” that has also made the Arctic “a safer place for America and its allies,” is how The Economist describes this news. Though the text is not public, the deal reportedly reaffirms much of the old deal, a 1951 pact that allowed the U.S. to freely operate military bases and traverse the icebound island.
What’s different, according to Mr. Trump, is that the U.S. will have the right to veto plans by its adversaries to build a military presence or undertake “sensitive investments” on the island. With China’s interest in investing in critical minerals projects, as well as the Russian navy’s use of Arctic waterways, this could protect Western Europe’s interests, too.
The timing of this agreement is significant for the transatlantic alliance, even in its current frayed state. Mr. Trump’s announcement came on the same day that Congress passed a Russia sanctions bill, which boosts Europe’s efforts to help Ukraine fend off aggression from Moscow. That same day marked the completion of NATO’s weeklong Arctic Shield military exercises, which included the U.S.
As a result of the deal, the U.S. military is expected to begin constructing new bases, while U.S. businesses plan to invest in minerals ventures. Earlier this month, in what some analysts see as a counter to U.S. influence, the European Union signed a €200 million investment plan with Danish and Greenlandic representatives.
On an island where climate, geography, and distance have long constrained economic growth and opportunities, these moves together signal a boon for Greenland’s approximately 56,000 inhabitants.
The territory’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, recently thanked the EU for helping Greenland address “challenges that we cannot tackle alone.” And of the latest deal with the U.S., he said simply, “It is for the benefit of us all.”
That’s a goal worth keeping in mind as the shifting Western alliance navigates global challenges, even in the frigid north.
